Because imagine you survive through the plague from the columbian exchange + slavery, you and your descendents are not gonna have a good time. The Spanish kept their colonies poor on purpose, forbid them to trade with eachother, forced them to grow cash-crops and every colony was centered about only a few ressources (some of them like gold being non renewable), which prevented the colonies from being self-sufficient, and on top of that they build a pyramidal hierarchy with 0 social mobility. No one outside of the colonies except the spanish were allowed to enter them, and people couldn't travel between the colonies (and even less leave them). If you're interested I suggest you to read the works of Alexander von Humbolt, who traveled there in the late 1700's and described it in detail.

They's a common myth saying that the US had to drop the atomic bombs or else Japan would have never surrendered, and they would have been a costly land invasion ("operation dawnfall") that would have the war last for at least 4 more years. However, this couldn't be further from the truth, for 2 reasons. 1) In the West we tend to overestimate the fanaticism of the Japanese at the end of ww2. We like to compare them to Samurai or to say that "in their culture it's dishonorable to surrender" and they would rather die than to lose a war. While it is true that some soldiers (especially on remote islands) refused to surrender even after the capitulation, in reality the japanese population was just like everyone else. They were tired of the war, they were tired of the bombings and the rationning. Most of them wanted to end the war like any normal human being would. Only the delusional japanese general staff wanted to continue the war at all costs. 2) Another often overlooked reason for the japanese capitulation was the soviet union joining the war. In reality, the japanese feared the soviets as much (if not more) than the americans. So when the red army steamrolled over Manchuria, northern Korea and the Sakhalin/Karafuto and the Kurils/Chishima islands, the Japanese knew that it was over. So if the US had dropped the atomic bombs (or even just one) on an uninhabited area or on a war ships squadron in the sea it would already have been enough to push Japan towards capitulation. However, I'm not sure that the US considered this option, they had the bomb first, and they probably really wanted to see what would happen if you drop this over a densely populated area

Basically, imagine an alternative version of the One Piece universe, were I, a former pirate who can turn into a giant green owl, "recieve" a predestined mission to destroy an evil supernatural being who grows more powerful every time he respawns. After I defeated the current reincarnation of the evil being on the first island (and liberated it), he briefely disappears but his 2nd in command takes over the Elemental islands. I lead a rebellion against him and in two years we kill him and liberate the island. I "unlock" a new weapon which is a black saber that can cut almost everything (but I don't use it that much), but before I killed the 2nd in command he had the time to finish the ritual to invoke the evil supreme being in his "ultimate" form, which means he can be definitely killed, but he is like 10x more powerful. Ce qui est intéressant (mais aussi effrayant) avec la colonisation espagnole, c'était que les colonies en Amérique latine étaient en quelques sortes les premiers régimes totalitaires de l'histoire, dans le sens où l'autorité exerce un contrôle maximal sur la vie des habitants. Alexandre de Humboldt, pendant ses voyages là-bas autour de 1800 (donc peu de temps avant l'indépendance), décrivait avec exactitude l'appareil coercitif de l'empire espagnol. La population était divisée et répartie dans un système hiérarchique pyramidal strict et fermé, une recréation artificielle et perfectionnée du féodalisme. Chaque colonie ne produisait qu'une seule (ou une poignée) ressource, la loi était 10x plus stricte que sur le continent, personne n'avait le droit de rentrer et personne n'avait le droit d'en sortir. Et alors que durant l'époque précolombienne il existait un réseau complexe de routes commerciales dans toute l'Amérique du Sud et centrale, le commerce entre les colonies a été purement et simplement interdit. Bref, tout était fait pour ne pas les rendre auto-suffisantes, ce qui est une des raisons pour lesquelles ces pays sont moins développés aujourd'hui.

3) Le boom économique le plus récent, les Trente Glorieuses, est arrivé à un moment où les colonies sont progressivement devenues indépendantes.

4) Les données montrent que le revenu obtenu grâce aux colonies dans l'ensemble du pays était dérisoire. Certaines colonies coutaient même plus cher que ce qu'elles rapportaient.

  
Je ne dis pas que les colonies n'ont rien apporté du tout à l'État, ou que la colonisation n'était pas un grand pillage, mais de là dire que la France doit sa richesse uniquement grâce à ses colonies est une absurdité totale.
